title: Paloma and the Parish
premise: Beatrix Ashgrove, the coroner of the parish town of Hollowmere, has quietly solved three deaths the police ruled accidental, earning her a reputation she never wanted. When local schoolteacher Paloma Vane disappears, Beatrix finds the woman's diary in an evidence box—entries continuing for weeks after her disappearance, written in handwriting that isn't quite hers. Following the diary's coded references, Beatrix uncovers a thirty-year-old cover-up involving the parish's beloved founding families, who faked Paloma's death to protect a secret about the church fire of 1994. As the statute of limitations on the original crime nears expiry, Beatrix must choose between exposing the truth and sparing the one person—the rector's widow—who once saved her own life. In the end, Beatrix forces a public reckoning at the parish harvest festival, the guilty confess, and Paloma is found alive in hiding, choosing to return not to duty but to the life she actually wants.
about_author: Petra Whitlock is the pen name of a former rural journalist who spent a decade covering small-town courtrooms and county funerals. She writes mysteries from a farmhouse kitchen table, where she keeps a ledger of every fictional death she has committed.

chapters.title: The Coroner Who Knew the Graves
chapters.summary: Beatrix Ashgrove performs her four-hundredth inquest, narrating the dead of Hollowmere by name and habit. A routine autopsy on a drowned farmhand reveals ligature marks the police report omits—her fourth 'accident' that isn't. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: quiet competence shadowed by loneliness; she trusts the dead more than the living.

chapters.title: Paloma Vane Is Missing
chapters.summary: Schoolteacher Paloma Vane fails to appear for the autumn term; the constable shrugs it off as a woman exercising her freedom. Beatrix notices Paloma's car still parked at the church with a parking ticket dated nine days prior. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: irritation hardening into unease—Hollowmere prefers its mysteries buried.

chapters.title: Evidence Box 12
chapters.summary: Searching the records room, Beatrix finds Paloma's diary logged as evidence from a break-in complaint, then sealed. The final entry is dated eleven days after her disappearance: 'He knows I copied it. If I stop writing, look under the altar.' POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the thrill of the hunt colliding with dread.

chapters.title: Handwriting That Isn't Hers
chapters.summary: Beatrix compares the late entries against old lesson plans: the slant is right, the loops wrong—a practiced forgery by someone who knew Paloma intimately. She visits the rector's widow, Edith Crane, who goes pale at the diary's mention and asks her to leave. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: first real fear; the town's kindness has teeth.

chapters.title: Under the Altar
chapters.summary: Beatrix searches St. Brannoc's and finds a loose flagstone hiding a tin box: photographs of the 1994 church fire, a child's shoe, and a list of five family names—including the Cranes. Someone watches her from the vestry door and flees. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: exhilaration curdling into exposure; she is now a target.

chapters.title: The Fire of 1994
chapters.summary: In the newspaper archive, Beatrix reconstructs the fire: officially an electrical fault, but a six-year-old girl was never accounted for, and the parish raised a memorial stone anyway. The five families all donated within a week. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: grief for a child no one mourned properly; her vocation as a voice for the dead deepens.

chapters.title: Constable Rennie's Debt
chapters.summary: Beatrix confronts young Constable Rennie, whose father signed the 1994 report. He admits his father drank himself to death over 'the lie,' and slips her the case file before warning her to stop. POV: alternating Beatrix and Rennie. Emotional beat: an unlikely alliance formed out of inherited guilt.

chapters.title: Edith's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Edith Crane invites Beatrix to tea and tells a partial truth: the fire killed no one—but something else happened that night, and Paloma found out while cataloguing parish records. Edith begs her to let sleeping graves lie. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: tenderness and betrayal intertwined; Edith once shielded teenage Beatrix from her father's violence.

chapters.title: Three Accidents, Revisited
chapters.summary: Rennie and Beatrix map her three earlier cases onto the five family names: each victim had been digging into the fire. The pattern confirms someone is still killing to keep the secret—and Paloma may be next, or already gone. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: cold clarity; this stopped being history the moment it started killing again.

chapters.title: The Diary's Last Author
chapters.summary: A graphologist friend identifies the forged entries' writer as left-handed with clerical training—narrowing to two men: the current rector, Simon Crane, or retired sexton Aldous Pike. That night Beatrix's cottage is searched. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: violation and resolve; invisibility is officially over.

chapters.title: What Paloma Copied
chapters.summary: Decoding Paloma's marginalia, Beatrix learns what she took from the parish archive: a birth record proving the 'dead' child of 1994 didn't die—she was given away to conceal her parentage among the five families. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the mystery pivots from murder to a life stolen twice.

chapters.title: Aldous Pike Digs Holes
chapters.summary: Beatrix tails the sexton to the old quarry at night and witnesses him burning papers. Confronted, he breaks: he forged the diary entries on Edith's orders—not to hide a murder, but to buy time because Paloma was hiding voluntarily. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: relief undercut by new questions—who is Paloma protecting?

chapters.title: Paloma's Letters
chapters.summary: Following quarry clues, Beatrix finds a cache of letters Paloma wrote but never sent—one addressed to Beatrix herself, saying: 'You of all people know what it costs to survive your own family.' POV: interlaced Beatrix and Paloma flashbacks. Emotional beat: recognition between two women shaped by secrets.

chapters.title: The Parentage of Ash
chapters.summary: DNA from the child's shoe matches a living descendant of the founding Harrow family—the child grew up locally under another name. Beatrix realizes the five families weren't covering a death; they were concealing an incestuous lineage and the baby born of it. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: revulsion and pity; respectability built on rot.

chapters.title: Statute of Limitations
chapters.summary: Rennie warns her: the obstruction charges expire in nineteen days, after which the conspiracy becomes untouchable. The five families convene an emergency parish council meeting and vote to have Beatrix removed as coroner. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the walls closing in; duty and belonging pull in opposite directions.

chapters.title: Edith Breaks
chapters.summary: Beatrix lays everything before Edith: the shoe, the letters, the statute clock. Edith confesses her role—she helped hide the child in 1994 to spare her own sister, and later helped Paloma disappear when the families threatened her. POV: Edith, framed by Beatrix. Emotional beat: love against duty made flesh; loyalty as both sin and salvation.

chapters.title: Where the Living Hide
chapters.summary: Edith gives up Paloma's location: a convent guesthouse on the coast where the grown 'dead' child—now Sister Ruth—has lived under vows since 1994. Beatrix drives through fog to find Paloma already there, waiting for her. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: breathless convergence; the missing woman chose her grave while alive.

chapters.title: Sister Ruth
chapters.summary: Paloma and Sister Ruth tell Beatrix the full story: Ruth learned her origins from the archive, Paloma copied proof to help her claim her name, and the families moved to silence them both. Ruth is ready to testify—if Beatrix can guarantee the town won't destroy her. POV: Paloma and Ruth. Emotional beat: courage offered conditionally; truth needs a protector.

chapters.title: Nineteen Days Become Two
chapters.summary: One of the five families, the Harrows, attempts one last 'accident'—a staged brake failure that nearly kills Rennie. Beatrix realizes waiting for the legal deadline means more bodies; they must move now, publicly, or not at all. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: fury transmuted into decision; the coroner chooses the living over procedure.

chapters.title: The Harvest Festival
chapters.summary: At the parish's biggest gathering, Beatrix takes the stage during the memorial wreath-laying and reads the 1994 record aloud, presenting Ruth—alive—to the entire town. The five families fracture; two elders confess on the spot to obstructing the original inquiry. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the climax—truth spoken in the one place duty cannot reach.

chapters.title: Reckonings
chapters.summary: Charges are filed just inside the statute; the rector resigns, the Harrow patriarch is arrested, and Edith accepts a suspended sentence with the town's grudging forgiveness. Beatrix is reinstated, offered a big-city post, and declines. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: justice imperfect but real; belonging earned rather than inherited.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Spring comes to Hollowmere. Beatrix walks the churchyard with Paloma, adding a true name to the memorial stone and closing her ledger of unsolved deaths. Paloma stays—as teacher, and perhaps as something more. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: resolution and warmth; the woman who knew every grave finally belongs among the living.
